title: Transports: stdio and Streamable HTTP
summary: MCP defines two transports. stdio runs a server as a local subprocess for one client. Streamable HTTP serves many clients from one endpoint. The older HTTP+SSE transport is Deprecated.
useIf: You must decide how a host reaches a server: spawn it locally, or call it as a shared network service.
avoidIf: You are tempted to start new work on HTTP+SSE or to put secrets on a local HTTP port with no Origin check.

explain.md: **stdio**: the client launches the server as a subprocess and exchanges newline-delimited JSON-RPC over stdin and stdout, with no embedded newlines. The server MUST NOT write anything but MCP messages to `stdout`. `stderr` is free for any logging and clients SHOULD NOT treat it as an error. The trust boundary is the operating-system process and its environment [[tr8]].

**Streamable HTTP** (2026-07-28): one MCP endpoint that accepts POST. Every JSON-RPC message is its own POST with an `Accept` header listing `application/json` and `text/event-stream`. The reply is one JSON object or a per-request SSE stream. Required headers include `MCP-Protocol-Version`, `Mcp-Method` and, for `tools/call`, `resources/read` and `prompts/get`, `Mcp-Name`. Servers MUST validate `Origin` (403 if invalid), SHOULD bind local servers to `127.0.0.1` and SHOULD send `X-Accel-Buffering: no` on SSE [[r2]].

In 2025-11-25 the same endpoint also supported GET and DELETE for a session, tied to an `Mcp-Session-Id` [[r22]]. In 2026-07-28 the GET stream and DELETE are gone, closing an SSE stream cancels the request, and long-lived notifications use one `subscriptions/listen` POST. The legacy **HTTP+SSE** transport (2024-11-05, a `/sse` stream plus a `/messages` endpoint) was replaced in 2025-03-26 and is Deprecated [[r9]].

explain.title: Choosing a transport
explain.alt: Decision flow: if the server runs on one user's machine for one client use stdio, otherwise use Streamable HTTP with OAuth and a gateway, and avoid legacy HTTP+SSE.
explain.src:
flowchart TD
  A{Server on one user's machine?} -->|yes| B{One client only?}
  B -->|yes| C[stdio subprocess]
  B -->|no| D[Streamable HTTP on 127.0.0.1]
  A -->|no| E[Streamable HTTP service]
  E --> F[OAuth, Origin check, gateway]

explain.title: Vendor support is not spec status
explain.md: OpenAI's remote MCP tool accepts Streamable HTTP or HTTP/SSE servers [[tr12]]. A host that still connects to `/sse` does not make HTTP+SSE current in the spec. Plan to Streamable HTTP.

whereToUse: stdio for developer tools that touch local files, git or a local database
Streamable HTTP for shared services owned by a platform team and used by many hosts
Streamable HTTP behind a gateway when you need rate limits, quotas and central logging
A localhost HTTP daemon when several local clients share one expensive process

use: Use stdio when one client owns one server process on one machine
Use Streamable HTTP when users, tenants or hosts differ from the operator
Use a gateway when governance needs central control
Use OAuth on remote servers for user-delegated access
avoid: Binding a local HTTP server to all interfaces
Writing logs to stdout on a stdio server
flips: Many users need the tool: move from stdio to a remote service with OAuth
Cold start per user is too slow: share a long-lived remote server

pitfalls.symptom: A stdio server fails to start in the host with parse errors
pitfalls.cause: A library or print statement wrote text to `stdout`
pitfalls.fix: Log to `stderr` only and keep `stdout` for MCP messages

pitfalls.symptom: A website can call a developer's local MCP server
pitfalls.cause: The HTTP server bound to all interfaces and skipped `Origin` validation, enabling DNS rebinding
pitfalls.fix: Bind to `127.0.0.1`, validate `Origin` (403) and require an auth token

pitfalls.symptom: Streamed progress arrives in bursts behind a reverse proxy
pitfalls.cause: The proxy buffered the SSE response
pitfalls.fix: Send `X-Accel-Buffering: no` and disable buffering for the MCP route

scenarios.title: A local file tool for one developer
scenarios.situation: A developer wants an assistant to search and edit files in a project on their own laptop. Nobody else will connect. Startup time is not a problem.
unknowns: Is the server code trusted and from a known source?
Does the host ask for consent before launching it?
scenarios.question: Which transport do you choose?

options.name: stdio subprocess launched by the host
options.why: No network surface, no token flow, and the process boundary limits who can talk to it.
options.tradeoff: The server runs with the user's privileges, so only run reviewed code.

options.name: Local HTTP server on 127.0.0.1 with a token
options.why: Allows several local clients to share it.
options.tradeoff: You now own Origin checks and port access control.

options.name: A remote Streamable HTTP service with OAuth
options.why: It exposes local files over a network and adds auth work for no sharing benefit.
options.tradeoff: Right when many users need the capability or the data is remote.

flips.if: Several local tools share one expensive index
The team wants the same tool for everyone
flips.then: Move to a remote service with OAuth.

scenarios.title: A shared tenant service with central controls
scenarios.situation: A platform team offers tools to hundreds of employees across several hosts. It needs per-user identity, rate limits and a central audit log.
unknowns: Do consumers need resources and prompts, or tools only?
scenarios.question: How do you expose the capability?

options.name: Remote Streamable HTTP server behind a gateway with OAuth
options.why: One endpoint, per-request auth, and the gateway applies limits and logging.
options.tradeoff: You operate a service and need to match the gateway's MCP feature coverage.

options.name: Remote Streamable HTTP server reached directly by hosts
options.why: Simplest to run and still OAuth protected.
options.tradeoff: Each service must implement its own limits and audit.

options.name: Spawn a stdio process per user through a web proxy
options.why: A proxy that spawns processes is an escalation path from web attacks to code execution and offers no central control.
options.tradeoff: stdio is right only when the client itself launches a local, reviewed server.

flips.if: Only one team consumes the server
flips.then: Skip the gateway and call it directly.

flips.if: Consumers need prompts and resources and the gateway supports tools only
flips.then: Reach the server directly or choose another gateway.

scenarios.takeaway: Shared, governed access needs a remote transport with real auth.

scenarios.title: An old `/sse` server in production
scenarios.situation: A server built from an early tutorial exposes `/sse` and `/messages`. Some hosts are newer and some are not. You can add endpoints but cannot update every host quickly.
unknowns: What share of traffic still uses `/sse`?
scenarios.question: What is the migration path?

options.name: Add a Streamable HTTP endpoint, keep `/sse` while you watch traffic, then retire it
options.why: Moves new clients to the supported transport with no breakage and metrics decide when to cut.
options.tradeoff: Two transports to maintain for a while.

options.name: Remove `/sse` today
options.why: Breaks every host that still uses it.
options.tradeoff: Right only when metrics show no legacy traffic.

options.name: Stay on HTTP+SSE only
options.tradeoff: Deprecated transport, and new hosts may stop supporting it.

flips.if: No client uses `/sse` for a full release cycle
A key host supports only HTTP+SSE
flips.then: Keep it for that host with a retirement date.

scenarios.takeaway: Run both transports until traffic data says the old one is dead.

quiz.q: A stdio MCP server crashes the host on connect. The server prints a startup banner with `print`. What is the cause?
options: The banner went to `stdout`, which must carry only MCP messages
quiz.explain: The server MUST NOT write anything but MCP messages to stdout, so the host fails to parse the banner. `stderr` is the correct place for logs. stdio uses JSON-RPC and has no 128-character limit.

quiz.q: A local Streamable HTTP server binds to 0.0.0.0 and does not check `Origin`. What attack does this enable?
quiz.explain: Without Origin validation and with a wide bind, a remote web page can use DNS rebinding to reach the local server. The others are different issues: passthrough is about tokens, shadowing about tool descriptions, and 2026-07-28 has no session id.

flashcards.front: What must a stdio MCP server never write to stdout?
flashcards.back: Anything except MCP messages. Use `stderr` for logs.

flashcards.front: How does Streamable HTTP work in 2026-07-28?
flashcards.back: One endpoint. Every JSON-RPC message is its own POST. The reply is a JSON object or a per-request SSE stream. GET and DELETE are gone.

flashcards.front: What is the status of HTTP+SSE?
flashcards.back: Deprecated. It was replaced by Streamable HTTP in 2025-03-26. Do not start new work on it.
